Hatchlings of the Eastern violet-backed sunbird emerge at a remarkably small body mass of 1.37 grams [Ww0 = 1.37 grams], a value typical of altricial passerines that require intensive parental care. The incubation period, which is sensitive to thermal conditions, lasts approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], a figure derived from comparative data on the closely related scarlet-chested sunbird. This relatively brief embryonic development is consistent with the energetic demands of a small-bodied nectivore that must balance thermoregulatory costs against the need to fledge offspring within a constrained breeding window. The mass at hatching represents only a fraction of the adult body weight, underscoring the substantial growth trajectory the nestling must undergo during the subsequent nestling phase. Field observations indicate that the newly hatched chicks are entirely dependent on the female for brooding and on both parents for the delivery of arthropod prey and nectar, a dietary shift that fuels the rapid tissue accretion characteristic of the early postnatal period. Adult females of this species attain a maximum recorded body mass of 10.3 grams [Wwi = 10.3 grams], a value that falls within the typical range of 8 to 12 grams reported for the species across its East African distribution. Body mass in adult females also fluctuates seasonally in response to nectar availability, with individuals accumulating fat reserves during the wet season to buffer against the resource scarcity of dry periods. Comparative measurements from museum specimens show that females are consistently heavier than males, a dimorphism likely linked to the metabolic demands of egg production and incubation. This sexual size difference is modest but measurable, and it may influence foraging niche partitioning within breeding pairs.

Investing in a single, well-provisioned clutch rather than multiple smaller broods may enhance offspring quality and post-fledging survival in a resource-limited environment.
